query: What minimum per-class and per-accent sample sizes (or power calculation) are needed to detect a target delta of 5–10% macro-F1 with 80% power for per-accent analyses?

response.query: What minimum per-class and per-accent sample sizes (or power calculation) are needed to detect a target delta of 5–10% macro-F1 with 80% power for per-accent analyses?
response.answer: To detect a 5-10% macro-F1 delta with 80% power, a minimum of 100-200 samples per accent class is needed. This assumes moderate effect size and standard significance level. Exact numbers depend on variance and effect size specifics.

results.title: G*Power Sample Size Calculation Guide for Statistical Tests - Studocu
results.content: One of the first articles was Cohen (1962)​ who found that the sample sizes used in articles only provided enough power to detect large effects (by Cohen’s guidelines a standardised mean difference of 0). Even experienced researchers overestimate the power provided by a given sample size, and underestimate the number of participants required for a given effect size (Bakker, Hartgerink, Wicherts, & van der Maas,​ 2016)​. “In order to detect an effect size of Cohen’s d = 0 with 80% power (alpha = .05, two-tailed), G\*Power suggests we would need 86 participants per groups (N = 172) in an independent samples t-test”. Selecting an effect size of interest for an *a priori* ​ power analysis would be an effective strategy if we wanted to calculate how many participants are required before the study began. This would tell us what effect sizes the study would be powered to detect in the long run for a given alpha, beta, and sample size. This could also be done for an *a priori* ​ power analysis, where you see the power curve for the number of participants rather than effect sizes. “An independent samples t-test with 40 participants per groups (N = 80) would be sensitive to effects of Cohen’s d = 0 with 80% power (alpha = .05, two-tailed). “In order to detect an effect size of Cohen’s *d* ​ = 0 with 80% power (alpha = .05, two-tailed), G\*Power suggests we would need 45 participants in a paired samples t-test”. If we change the type of power analysis to sensitivity, we can see what effect sizes a within-subjects design is sensitive enough to detect. “A paired samples t-test with 30 participants would be sensitive to effects of Cohen’s d = 0 with 80% power (alpha = .05, two-tailed). We would now need 339 participants (113 per group) to detect the effect with 80% power. ● Power (1 - β err prob) - Perhaps we do not want to miss out on detecting the effect 20% of the time in the long run, and wanted to conduct the test with greater sensitivity.

results.title: How to decide your sample size when the power calculation is not straightforward | NC3Rs
results.content:
Title: How to decide your sample size when the power calculation is not straightforward | NC3Rs
A question I’m most often asked (other than excluding those pesky outliers) is “what is a suitable sample size for my experiment?”. You cannot simply copy someone else’s sample sizes; you need to assess the variability of data generated in your lab, under your experimental conditions and using your protocols. Power curves are a useful visual tool to assess sample size and power for various biologically relevant effects. In the figure below, it can be seen that in order to achieve a statistical power of 80% (Y-axis), where the effect size is an absolute change of size 3 (green line), n=8 animals will be required (reading down to the X-axis). If the effect size you are interested in detecting is an absolute change of less than 2 (blue line), it will not be possible to power the experiment correctly. Power curves showing the sample sizes required to achieve different levels of statistical power with particular effect sizes. In deciding on the effect size that would be of biological relevance, one key question to ask is: what is the minimum effect I would need to see to consider it worth taking forward in further research? The statistical power will be higher (and the results more reliable) as the sample size is now three times greater. However, this is still not ideal and a more effective approach is to use a block design (each small experiment being a block) and calculate the sample size needed for the entire experiment with a power calculation. In this scenario, it may be possible to use fewer animals than in the three separate experiments while increasing the statistical power. With a group-sequential design, interim analyses, usually two or three, are pre-planned into the study design and experiments can be terminated early if a statistically significant effect has been achieved (or no effect observed), thus saving animals. For example, it turns out that if you are interested in understanding the dose-response relationship, and want to identify the ED50, then using a design with more dose groups and fewer animals per group, perhaps as low as three per group, is a better design to use than more orthodox designs/sample sizes.
